title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor
authors: Lucio Anderlini, Pietro Asinari, Gianluca Bertaina, Davide Calonico, Marco Coïsson, Alessio Gianelle
abstract: The identification of heavy-flavor jets, i.e. collimated streams of particles originating from the fragmentation of beauty and charm quarks produced in proton-proton collisions, represents one of the most challenging classification tasks in measurements at Large Hadron Collider experiments. In recent years, advanced machine learning techniques have been successfully employed to address this problem, while quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative approach. However, the high dimensionality of the problem, typically involving hundreds of observables, raises an open question: whether the current generation of quantum computers, characterized by limited qubit count, can effectively tackle such complex tasks. In this work, a variational quantum circuit for the classification of b- and c-jets at the LHCb experiment is implemented on a 5-qubit superconducting quantum computer manufactured by IQM and installed at the Politecnico di Torino. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a quantum algorithm for jet identification using simulated data from an LHC experiment in which all stages of the machine-learning workflow, including training and testing, are performed on real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that the impact of hardware-induced quantum noise does not significantly degrade the performance. A framework for the evaluation of the training time on the quantum hardware and for the circuit optimization is also proposed. These findings pave the way for future applications on larger quantum devices based on superconducting qubits, featuring a larger number of qubits enabling the encoding of information beyond the reach of classical simulation and providing a step toward investigating whether quantum advantage may eventually be achievable in high-energy physics classification tasks.

infographic.key_insight: A 5-qubit superconducting processor demonstrated end-to-end quantum training and testing for beauty-versus-charm jet identification, with hardware noise reported not to significantly degrade performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study provides a practical workflow for hardware-based quantum classification, including training-time evaluation and circuit optimization.
method: Use simulated LHCb data to classify beauty and charm jets.
Implement a variational quantum circuit on an IQM 5-qubit superconducting processor.
Perform both training and testing on real quantum hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on simulated LHCb jet data found no significant performance degradation from hardware-induced noise, though the abstract gives no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The small-scale demonstration does not establish quantum advantage; scaling to high-dimensional jet data on larger devices remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor

title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
authors: Aritra Lahiri, Florian Marquardt
abstract: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM-based agent evolves programs that generate fault-tolerant Clifford circuits, guided by a circuit verifier.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce manual circuit-design effort across logical state preparation, logical gates, and encoded-qubit routines.
method: Frame circuit discovery as agentic evolutionary program synthesis.
Use an LLM’s pretrained knowledge and tool use to evolve circuit-generating programs.
Guide synthesis with a verifier and exhaustively check faults.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports fault-tolerant circuits for all curated tasks, including code switching and code growth, with each circuit verified by exhaustive fault checks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish scalability beyond curated tasks or specify the fault model and computational cost of exhaustive verification.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits

title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh, Román Orús, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A 145,281-parameter multi-head quantum module replaced eight transformer blocks in a 30-billion-parameter LLM, displacing 16.33% of its parameters with limited accuracy loss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Partitioning hidden states into small quantum heads enables NISQ-compatible integration into production-scale LLM architectures without encoding the full hidden width in one circuit.
method: Split 2,048 hidden dimensions into 32 heads using 8-qubit, 4-layer angle-encoded circuits.
Couple quantum heads through constrained classical linear mixers and learned readouts.
Train with exact statevector simulation, then execute quantum heads on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor.
infographic.evidence_signal: Held-out perplexity ablations found mixers alone within 1–3% of the full module for fused spans, while a parameter-matched classical MLP remained a few percent ahead.
infographic.watch_item: Quantum advantage is unproven: limited-seed non-entangling and frozen-circuit controls beat the full module, and hardware execution does not establish end-to-end speedup.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM

title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
authors: Tiago de Souza Farias, Caio Moraes Porto, Matheus da Silva Fonseca, Nicolas Armando Cabrera Carpi, Anderson de Araujo Oliveira, Celso Jorge Villas-Boas
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

infographic.key_insight: A frozen, general-purpose LLM can propose promising quantum circuit parameters for structured Hamiltonians, but performs worse than Adam optimization on general random Hamiltonians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM-generated circuit parameters offer independently evaluable energy estimates, unlike direct energy predictions that may violate physical bounds.
method: Generate complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions.
Optionally refine parameters using iterative energy feedback.
Evaluate random, structured parent, and molecular Hamiltonians; probe blind circuit interpretation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations found larger energy errors than Adam for general Hamiltonians, limited gains from feedback, and promising low-energy configurations for structured Hamiltonians.
infographic.watch_item: Do not assume reliable optimization across problems; independently evaluate generated parameters and check direct energy predictions against spectral bounds.
infographic.paper_title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models

title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding
authors: Yuki Sato, Ruho Kondo
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.

infographic.key_insight: An explicit block-encoding of the shifted finite element stiffness matrix enables a resource-efficient quantum framework for 2D isotropic linear elasticity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework identifies conditions for polynomial quantum speedups in preparing displacement states, estimating strain energy, and reconstructing low-resolution displacements.
method: Analytically diagonalize element stiffness matrices and factorize global finite element assembly.
Construct normalized block-encoding with constant ancilla qubits and gate complexity logarithmic in the degrees of freedom.
Apply a quantum singular value transformation-based linear system solver.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical cantilever beam experiments verify circuit accuracy and show agreement with conventional finite element solutions.
infographic.watch_item: Speedups are conditional and task-specific; low-resolution displacement reconstruction does not establish efficient recovery of the full classical solution.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding

title: A Unified Benchmarking Study of Variational Quantum Eigensolver Ansatz for Electronic Structure Problems
authors: Julie Maria Raju, Abhoy Kole, Julen Larrucea, Kamalika Datta, Lennart Weingarten, Rolf Drechsler
abstract: Electronic structure calculations become computationally expensive on classical computers as electron correlation increases. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative through hybrid quantum-classical Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) on Noisy-Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. The choice of ansatz plays a pivotal role in the performance and scalability of the VQE, yet selecting an optimal ansatz remains challenging. Existing approaches including chemically inspired ansatz, adaptive schemes and Hardware Efficient Ansätze (HEA) lack a unified comparison. This gap makes the scalability and trade-offs of each method unclear for varying molecular sizes. This work presents a systematic benchmarking study comparing Unitary Couples Cluster Singles and Doubles Ansatz (UCCSD), fermionic ADAPT-VQE, BasicPCA HEA, and Excitation Preserving HEA across molecules of varying size like $H_2$, $LiH$, $N_2$. We evaluate trade-offs among circuit depth, parameter count, ground-state energy error, and NISQ feasibility. ADAPT-VQE achieves accuracy comparable to UCCSD with lower resource overhead, but becomes impractical for modest system sizes ($\sim$10 electrons) due to increasing circuit complexity. In contrast, HEA reduces hardware costs but requires more parameters and sacrifices accuracy, with performance strongly dependent on molecular size. The Excitation Preserving ansatz remains below chemical accuracy for $H_2$ and $LiH$, and fails for $N_2$, underscoring the need to balance expressibility and trainability. Overall, these results highlight key trade-offs between accuracy and resource efficiency across VQE ansätze, emphasizing the need to improve ADAPT-VQE scalability and HEA accuracy while addressing optimization challenges for near-term quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: VQE ansatz selection trades accuracy for hardware cost: ADAPT-VQE approaches UCCSD accuracy with lower resource overhead, while hardware-efficient ansätze sacrifice accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Near-term electronic-structure workflows must balance circuit depth, parameter count, and optimization difficulty rather than choose an ansatz on accuracy alone.
method: Compare UCCSD, fermionic ADAPT-VQE, BasicPCA HEA, and Excitation Preserving HEA.
Benchmark electronic-structure calculations for H₂, LiH, and N₂.
Evaluate ground-state energy error, circuit depth, parameter count, and NISQ feasibility.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the tested molecules, ADAPT-VQE achieves accuracy comparable to UCCSD, while hardware-efficient ansatz performance depends strongly on molecular size.
infographic.watch_item: ADAPT-VQE becomes impractical around 10 electrons as circuit complexity grows, limiting its scalability despite favorable accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: A Unified Benchmarking Study of Variational Quantum Eigensolver Ansatz for Electronic Structure Problems

title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Xulong Tang, Narges Alavisamani, Joan Camps, Matthew Cha, Elise Jennings, Jack O'Connor
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction. In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels. We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information. We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration. It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical quantum error correction can organize decoding across cooperating decoder stages or multiple code levels, with distinct throughput and latency trade-offs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Practical fault-tolerant systems must match decoder architecture and hardware to syndrome workloads and quantum-control timing requirements.
method: Classify decoder-level and code-level hierarchies.
Review cascaded, windowed, streaming, and distributed decoding.
Compare cross-level information exchange and CPU, GPU, FPGA, ASIC, and cryogenic platforms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a literature review under reported evaluation conditions, not a new benchmark, and provides no quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Gaps in performance reporting and system integration limit direct comparisons and confidence in deployment readiness.
infographic.paper_title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction

title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch
authors: Dantong Li
abstract: The quantum switch applies two operations in a coherent superposition of their causal orders and is a simple example of indefinite causal order. No quantum circuit that uses each operation once in a definite order can even describe it, yet photonic experiments have demonstrated its physical realization. We ask how many calls to the black-box operations a quantum computer in the circuit model needs to reproduce the switch. If one of the black boxes is known to be unitary, three calls suffice. For general channels on a $d$-dimensional system, we prove three results. In all three, circuits may use classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory. First, no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. Second, approximation to any fixed error below $1/2$, measured in half the diamond norm, requires $Ω(d^{1/4})$ calls, exponential in the number of qubits. Third, an ordinary circuit can require exponentially many calls to obtain a single bit that the switch extracts with a few uses. We consider a device whose actual noise is dephasing in a fixed unknown basis and test it against a theoretical depolarizing model. The two channels have the same entanglement and average gate fidelities, so these figures alone do not distinguish them. At fixed noise strength, the quantum switch tells them apart with a number of device uses independent of $d$, whereas the circuit model requires $Ω(d^{1/16})$ calls. Noise characterization is needed for quantum error correction, and this gives a provable query advantage of the switch in a task relevant to practical quantum computing. We invite future work that extends such advantages to more practical computing tasks.

infographic.key_insight: The quantum switch offers provable query advantages over definite-order circuits: exact simulation of general channels is impossible with finitely many calls in the worst case.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its ability to distinguish noise models with identical entanglement and average gate fidelities could inform noise characterization for quantum error correction.
method: Analyze circuit-model simulation of coherently controlled operation orders.
Prove query lower bounds allowing classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory.
Compare unknown-basis dephasing with a theoretical depolarizing channel.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical bounds show Ω(d^{1/4}) calls for simulation below 1/2 half-diamond-norm error and Ω(d^{1/16}) for noise discrimination, versus dimension-independent switch uses for the latter.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract establishes theoretical query advantages, not experimentally validated performance gains under realistic implementation overheads.
infographic.paper_title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch

title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Optimization for CVRPTW: A Systems Framework with Provable Feasibility and Empirical Hardware Limits
authors: Syamasundar Gopasana, Swatantra Singh, Rohan Joydhar, Shubhashis Sengupta
abstract: Solving large-scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems with Time Windows (CVRPTW) remains challenging because strict operational constraints and scale limit both exact and heuristic methods. We present a hybrid classical-quantum architecture combining Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) with vehicle-level Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), solved using Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald quantum processors. The decomposition avoids the variable growth and constraint-enforcement difficulties of monolithic CVRPTW QUBO formulations. We evaluate the framework on five realistic benchmarks derived from London traffic and location data, spanning 10--70 customers, using a validation pipeline enforcing feasibility and monotone improvement over classical baselines. SQBM+ achieves verified fleet-distance reductions of 2.80% (7,927 m) for the 25-customer instance and 0.22% (1,186 m) for the 55-customer instance. QAOA experiments establish a current hardware boundary for reliable constraint satisfaction at subproblems of up to 4 customers (16 qubits). Diagnostic results identify assignment-level time-window tightness, rather than local route optimization, as the dominant scalability bottleneck. The results demonstrate a practical near-term role for hybrid classical-quantum optimization while establishing empirical limits for current quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid MILP–QUBO framework delivers verified routing improvements while identifying a current QAOA hardware boundary of 4 customers per subproblem (16 qubits).
infographic.engineering_relevance: Vehicle-level decomposition offers a practical way to test quantum optimization within capacity- and time-window-constrained routing without relying on monolithic QUBO formulations.
method: Combine classical MILP with vehicle-level QUBO route optimization.
Solve QUBOs using Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald.
Validate feasibility and accept only improvements over classical baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five London-derived benchmarks with 10–70 customers, SQBM+ reduced verified fleet distance by 2.80% (7,927 m) for 25 customers and 0.22% (1,186 m) for 55 customers.
infographic.watch_item: Assignment-level time-window tightness remains the main scalability bottleneck; the reported distance gains come from SQBM+, not evidence of quantum hardware advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Optimization for CVRPTW: A Systems Framework with Provable Feasibility and Empirical Hardware Limits

title: Hybrid Krotov gradient descent Optimization for Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Maximilian Fröhlich, Martin Eigel, Michael Hintermüller
abstract: We introduce and study a Krotov-inspired discrete adjoint optimization scheme for quantum machine learning and focus on a hybrid online-to-batch schedule. The method transfers the forward/costate/local-update logic of continuous-time optimal control to parameterized quantum circuits by replacing time locality with gate-index locality. For a broad class of fixed-generator variational gates and terminal-state losses, we show that the batch Krotov direction coincides with the exact gradient of the empirical loss. Under standard smoothness assumptions, this yields monotonic descent and convergence of the batch method, and convergence of the tail of the hybrid method after a finite switch to the batch phase. Empirically, we benchmark hybrid Krotov against the tuned PennyLane optimizer suite and L-BFGS-B on a four-bit parity classifier and on the Pérez-Salinas data re-uploading classifier for the crown problem. Across matched hyperparameter sweeps with three seeds per configuration, hybrid Krotov dominates every tuned first-order baseline and matches the strongest structured PennyLane methods on parity, while approaching the accuracy of L-BFGS-B on Pérez-Salinas at first-order per-iteration cost.

infographic.key_insight: A Krotov-inspired hybrid optimizer transfers optimal-control updates to quantum circuits, with a batch direction equal to the exact empirical-loss gradient for fixed-generator gates and terminal-state losses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a first-order-cost training alternative for variational quantum classifiers, with batch-phase descent and convergence guarantees under standard smoothness assumptions.
method: Replace time-local control updates with gate-index-local circuit updates.
Use forward-state propagation, costate propagation, and local parameter updates.
Switch from online updates to batch optimization after a finite initial phase.
infographic.evidence_signal: Matched hyperparameter sweeps with three seeds per configuration on four-bit parity and the Pérez-Salinas crown classifier showed stronger performance than tuned first-order PennyLane baselines on parity and accuracy approaching L-BFGS-B on the crown task.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees depend on the specified gate/loss structure and smoothness assumptions; the two small classification benchmarks do not establish large-scale or hardware performance.
infographic.paper_title: Hybrid Krotov gradient descent Optimization for Quantum Machine Learning

title: Structure makes quantum circuits trainable
authors: Wenbo Xie, Wojciech Szpankowski, Ananth Grama
abstract: The scalability of variational quantum algorithms is limited by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially in system size. This worst-case result raises fundamental questions about the trainability of quantum AI models. We present a major advance towards resolving this trainability question by answering whether a given quantum circuit has a barren plateau. We do this using an analytical framework that bounds the gradient variance for arbitrary input states $ρ$ and observables $\mathcal{M}$ by decomposing the unitary representation of the associated compact Lie group. When the circuit segments on both sides of a gate form $2$-designs, we obtain the variance exactly and prove a sufficient condition for trainability: if $ρ^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\otimes 2}$ are sufficiently concentrated on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension, and the differentiated gate moves this subspace by an inverse-polynomial amount, then the gradient variance is at least inverse-polynomial. We further present a sampling algorithm that estimates the gradient variance from runs of the ansatz, without constructing the representation-theoretic projectors. Our algorithm decides whether the variance exceeds a tolerance $τ$ with the number of runs polynomial in $1/τ$, including cases in which the bounds are inconclusive. This resolves the question of the trainability of the circuit before expensive training procedures.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum circuits can avoid barren plateaus when input and observable structure align within a polynomial-dimensional invariant subspace that the differentiated gate moves sufficiently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can help assess circuit trainability before expensive optimization and guide ansatz design toward nonvanishing gradient variance.
method: Decompose the circuit’s compact Lie group representation to bound gradient variance for arbitrary inputs and observables.
Derive exact variance when circuit segments on both sides of the differentiated gate form 2-designs.
Estimate variance from ansatz runs without constructing representation-theoretic projectors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical variance bounds, a sufficient trainability condition, and a sampling algorithm using polynomially many runs in inverse tolerance, but no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The trainability condition is sufficient, not necessary, and sampling costs may become large for very small variance tolerances.
infographic.paper_title: Structure makes quantum circuits trainable

title: Training quantum neural networks one job at a time
authors: Muhammad Faryad, Rabab Alomairy
abstract: When a quantum processor is reached through a cloud queue, a variational algorithm pays for every round trip, and a single round trip can carry many circuits. The classical optimizer therefore decides how much is learned per job, not only per shot. We study this for a quantum neural network classifier. We compare optimizers that are given the same number of jobs and the same shots per job, and that differ only in how they fill each job. This comparison treats hybrid quantum-classical training as an execution-efficiency problem: how to obtain useful optimization progress from each costly interaction with a quantum processor. The resulting perspective connects optimizer design to overhead amortization and efficient use of accelerator resources. A direct port of a batched pattern search that worked for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm stalls once the model has a few dozen parameters. What does transfer is the principle behind it: fill each job with a batch of parameter vectors that is fixed before the job is sent. For circuits built from Pauli rotations the natural batch is the parameter-shift stencil. We show that its gradient error falls as the inverse of the shots per job, while the error of simultaneous-perturbation methods (SPSA) has a floor that no number of shots removes. In simulation, batched parameter-shift training needs between a fifth and a half of the jobs SPSA needs, for 24 to 48 parameters, and the ordering holds at two noise levels. A new structure-aware stencil search reads the same kind of rows as sinusoids and also beats SPSA. On IBM's ibm_fez processor, in three interleaved runs at six and eight qubits, the batched optimizer reached SPSA's final training loss within 4 to 20 of its 50 jobs. Its test accuracy was clearly higher at eight qubits; at six qubits the difference was not significant. All hardware numbers can be re-derived from the raw shots.

infographic.key_insight: Batching parameter-shift evaluations into each quantum job accelerates quantum neural network training under matched job and shot budgets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizer design should maximize useful progress per cloud submission, not just per shot, to amortize quantum-processor access overhead.
method: Compare optimizers using equal job counts and shots per job.
Preassemble parameter-shift batches to estimate gradients in one submission.
Test a structure-aware stencil search that interprets evaluations as sinusoids.
infographic.evidence_signal: For 24–48 parameters, simulated parameter-shift training needed 20–50% as many jobs as SPSA; across three interleaved IBM hardware runs at six and eight qubits, it matched SPSA’s final training loss in 4–20 versus 50 jobs.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware evidence is limited to six- and eight-qubit models, and the test-accuracy advantage was not significant at six qubits.
infographic.paper_title: Training quantum neural networks one job at a time

title: Quantum Material Generation via Coherent Hamiltonian Search
authors: Jiang Yuhan, Matthew Otten
abstract: Discovering new materials with targeted properties is a central goal of materials science, yet the space of candidates is vast. Data-driven generative models learn the distribution of known materials, but they extrapolate poorly, and a generated structure is not known to be stable. A material's properties follow from its Hamiltonian, and a quantum computer can calculate them from it. We introduce the quantum material generative algorithm (QMage), a coherent search, guided by the Hamiltonian, over crystalline configurations of atomic composition, unit cell structure, and atomic positions, for one whose calculated properties meet the targets to within a given error tolerance. The computation is a single coherent quantum circuit in which each configuration's Hamiltonian is block-encoded, its target eigenstate isolated and properties evaluated, and the satisfying configurations amplified by fixed-point search and measured. One framework covers many targets, from formation energy and band gaps to elasticity and conductivity. We design the algorithm for the mature fault-tolerant era and estimate its cost in logical qubits and Toffoli depth from a classically routine benchmark to targets where established methods are unreliable. The approach generates candidate materials from first principles, rather than generalizing from those known, and could enable materials discovery when the target properties are difficult to predict classically.

infographic.key_insight: QMage proposes a coherent quantum search for crystal configurations whose Hamiltonian-derived properties meet specified targets within an error tolerance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support first-principles materials discovery for properties that are difficult to predict classically, but requires mature fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
method: Search over atomic compositions, unit cell structures, and atomic positions.
Block-encode each configuration’s Hamiltonian, isolate a target eigenstate, and evaluate material properties.
Amplify configurations meeting property targets using fixed-point search, then measure candidates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports logical-qubit and Toffoli-depth cost estimates spanning a classically routine benchmark to targets where established methods are unreliable, rather than experimental materials validation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical feasibility depends on fault-tolerant resource demands and reliable eigenstate preparation; satisfying selected property targets does not automatically establish material stability.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Material Generation via Coherent Hamiltonian Search

title: Max-Cut QAOA on Non-Hardware-Native Graphs via MinLA Surrogates and Configuration Recovery
authors: K. Bharati, Nathan Earnest-Noble, Ritajit Majumdar
abstract: For non-hardware-native \textsc{MAX-CUT} instances, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can incur additional two-qubit depth overhead due to SWAP-based routing of interactions between non-adjacent qubits. We propose a hybrid quantum--classical workflow that reduces this depth by selectively removing interactions and subsequently recovers solution quality through classical optimization of the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective. We employ a Minimum Linear Arrangement (MinLA)-based vertex ordering to preferentially retain short-range interactions, thereby constructing a two-qubit depth-reduced surrogate QAOA ansatz. To compensate for the information lost through interaction removal, we develop classical \textit{recovery} strategies that refine QPU-sampled bitstrings directly on the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective. We develop two recovery strategies: signed-residue-based local search and bipartite-block optimization, where each conditional block problem is solved exactly using an $s$--$t$ minimum cut. Recovery is performed independently on each sampled configuration, ensuring monotonic improvement in cut value without additional QPU executions. We evaluate the workflow on \texttt{ibm\_kingston} for 120 distinct non-hardware-native instances comprising $6$-regular and Erdős--Rényi graphs with 40, 60 and 100 vertices. We verify that the surrogates substantially reduce transpiled two-qubit depth while staying within the prescribed two-qubit depth, and with recovery yield \textit{near-optimal} cuts on the original graphs. These results demonstrate the potential of hardware-aware interaction selection and classical recovery to extend QAOA to graph instances whose full cost Hamiltonians exceed practical circuit-depth budgets.

infographic.key_insight: MinLA-guided interaction removal reduces QAOA circuit depth, while classical recovery improves sampled solutions on the original Max-Cut graph without additional QPU executions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow helps fit non-hardware-native Max-Cut instances within practical two-qubit depth budgets by trading quantum interactions for classical postprocessing.
method: Use a Minimum Linear Arrangement ordering to preferentially retain short-range graph interactions.
Run QAOA with the depth-reduced surrogate cost Hamiltonian.
Refine each sampled bitstring using signed-residue local search or bipartite-block optimization with exact conditional min-cut solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on ibm_kingston covered 120 non-hardware-native 6-regular and Erdős–Rényi graphs with 40, 60, and 100 vertices, reporting substantial two-qubit depth reductions and near-optimal recovered cuts.
infographic.watch_item: Monotonic recovery guarantees nondecreasing cut values, not global optimality; performance beyond the tested graph families and hardware remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Max-Cut QAOA on Non-Hardware-Native Graphs via MinLA Surrogates and Configuration Recovery

title: Phase Interference and Transverse Catalysts Govern the Noise Fragility of Long-Range Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Longhui Shen, Fangzhou Jin, Xiaoxia Yi, Bin Guo
abstract: Long-range entangling gates shorten variational state preparation, but they also accelerate operator spreading across the register, linking nonlocality to a presumed noise fragility. Here we show that the single-fault fragility $F$ of a variational circuit is governed by how fault phases interfere on the target Hamiltonian, not by how far faults spread. For Heisenberg chains we prove that two faults with identical extensive support can incur either bounded or extensive energy damage, in the exact ratio $N/2$. A phase-matched longitudinal halo remains energetically dark until ignited by transverse catalysts that break a symmetry of the remote register, namely spatially nonuniform single-qubit rotations or the pair-flip component of two-qubit $XX/YY$ gates, whereas uniform rotations and magnetization-conserving exchange gates leave it strictly dark. In noisy training with full-width long-range $ZZ$ gates, suppressing either catalyst alone leaves circuits trapped on an ignited plateau sustained by remote $XY$ couplings, whereas suppressing both eliminates the plateau, achieves minimal fragility despite larger fault operators, and halves the dephasing error. Training is driven by a race between catalyst pruning and gradient force balance, as annealing the transverse catalysts out of trapped circuits rescues every trajectory while annealing the entire longitudinal sector does not. Combined with the gate-count exposure $λ=pK$, a single fragility measurement accurately predicts the noise-induced energy shift across circuit architectures and noise strengths, reducing ansatz design to a trade-off between coherent expressivity and gate count.

infographic.key_insight: Long-range variational circuits are fragile when fault phases interfere destructively with target-energy performance, not simply when faults spread widely.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ansatz design should balance expressivity and gate-count exposure while controlling transverse catalysts that activate otherwise energetically dark faults.
method: Prove contrasting energy damage for equally extensive faults in Heisenberg chains.
Compare noisy training with nonuniform rotations and pair-flip gate components suppressed separately or together.
Predict noise-induced energy shifts using single-fault fragility and gate-count exposure λ = pK.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an exact N/2 energy-damage ratio for equally extensive faults, halved dephasing error when both catalysts are suppressed, and rescue of every tested trapped trajectory by annealing transverse catalysts.
infographic.watch_item: The reported mechanisms concern Heisenberg chains and specified circuit and noise settings; broader hardware and Hamiltonian generalization needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Phase Interference and Transverse Catalysts Govern the Noise Fragility of Long-Range Variational Quantum Circuits

title: Formulating Uncomputation Beyond Classical Ancilla Use
authors: Bonan Su, Shengyuan Yang
abstract: Ancilla qubits are routinely used to simplify quantum circuit construction and reduce implementation costs, but their use introduces the burden of designing proper uncomputation afterward. To alleviate this, prior work has developed automated uncomputation synthesis based on a computational-basis formulation of ancilla use. However, this formulation is tailored to classically structured ancilla computations. For more general circuits, it may be undefined, yield unintended functionality, or fail to synthesize uncomputation. It therefore falls short of providing a precise and general formulation of uncomputation beyond classical ancilla use. To address these limitations, we propose a new formulation of ancilla use that specifies the operation of each gate through two complementary aspects: (1) the functionality it implements and (2) the transformation it induces on ancilla roles. Based on this specification, we define uncomputation as restoring the initial ancilla role while implementing the identity functionality. This perspective enables a simple Use-first strategy for automatically synthesizing uncomputation in cases both within and beyond the scope of prior approaches. We further develop a complete inference system for reasoning about specifications, together with a derivation-directed procedure for automatically synthesizing efficient uncomputation, enabling systematic uncomputation synthesis even in challenging cases beyond the scope of our automatic strategy.

infographic.key_insight: Uncomputation can extend beyond classically structured ancilla use by restoring initial ancilla roles while implementing identity functionality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This formulation could broaden automated ancilla cleanup in quantum circuit compilation beyond cases supported by computational-basis approaches.
method: Specify each gate by its functionality and its transformation of ancilla roles.
Apply a Use-first strategy to automatically synthesize uncomputation.
Use a complete inference system and derivation-directed synthesis for more challenging cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports formal completeness and synthesis methods, but provides no quantitative benchmarks or hardware evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical scalability and circuit-cost improvements remain unquantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Formulating Uncomputation Beyond Classical Ancilla Use

title: Observing Enhanced Entanglement in an Ising Quantum Register Beyond Weak Measurement
authors: K. G. S. H. Gunawardana
abstract: Measurements often yield a disentangled quantum state which is the most probable measurement outcome while the measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement could be exponentially less probable or absent. Higher probability in measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement is virtue in experimental observation of enhance entanglement in post-selected or Born-rule measurements with less resources in noisy quantum devices. We develop a periodic measurement sampling(PMS) protocol in the framework of uniform matrix product states. Using PMS, we identify a peak enhancement of entanglement in a uniform post-measurement state whose probabilistic outcome can be maximized by optimizing a measurement super-cell. A measurement super-cell is the smallest repeating building block of qubits defined by the measurement density, external field strength and exchange interactions between quantum register and ancilla qubits. The above prediction based on a classical description of the many-body quantum state is demonstrated in a quantum computing experiment in a loop of quantum register qubits with Ising interactions in the presence of transverse magnetic field. Further, we show the scalability of predictions of the periodic measurement sampling protocol in the thermodynamic limit to finite size systems. Especially, we present a rescaling ansatz which would enable predicting the possibility of observing enhanced entanglement in finite size systems.

infographic.key_insight: Periodic measurement sampling identifies entanglement-enhancing outcomes in an Ising quantum register and optimizes their probability through a repeating measurement super-cell.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing measurement patterns could reduce the experimental resources needed to observe enhanced entanglement on noisy quantum devices.
method: Model periodic measurements using uniform matrix product states.
Optimize a measurement super-cell defined by measurement density, field strength, and register–ancilla interactions.
Use a rescaling ansatz to connect thermodynamic-limit predictions to finite systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a quantum computing demonstration on a transverse-field Ising qubit loop and finite-size scalability analysis, but gives no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical resource savings remain unquantified in the abstract and may depend on device noise and post-selection success rates.
infographic.paper_title: Observing Enhanced Entanglement in an Ising Quantum Register Beyond Weak Measurement

title: Recursive Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz
authors: Lennart Binkowski, Stuart Flannigan
abstract: The recursive quantum approximate optimisation algorithm~(RQAOA) shrinks an unconstrained combinatorial optimisation problem by eliminating one variable at a time, guided by correlations measured in variational quantum states. We extend this recursion to constrained problems by building on the quantum alternating operator ansatz, which restricts the evolution to feasible solutions through a feasible initial state and feasibility-preserving mixers. However, every elimination alters the feasibility structure, so that such a mixer for the original problem generally fails to be one for the subproblems. Previous extensions to Maximum Independent Set and Minimum Vertex Cover sidestep this with tailored reduction rules that keep every subproblem within the original problem class. We resolve this by identifying, for a given constraint structure, a broader problem class that is closed under all eliminations, and by efficiently constructing feasible initial states and feasibility-preserving mixers for every class member. We do so for monotone constraints, such as for the knapsack problem, for linear equality constraints with polynomially bounded weights, including Hamming weight constraints, and for combinations of equality constraints with a single inequality constraint, such as the cardinality-constrained knapsack problem. Conversely, we show that these restrictions cannot be lifted in general without leaving the realm of efficient constructions. Exact simulations on knapsack and vertex-weighted max-bisection instances demonstrate that our recursive scheme can outperform both its non-recursive counterpart and penalty-based QAOA and RQAOA.

infographic.key_insight: Recursive quantum optimisation can handle constrained problems by using broader problem classes that remain closed under variable elimination.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables recursive optimisation for problems such as knapsack and fixed-cardinality selection while keeping quantum evolution within feasible solutions.
method: Use correlations from variational quantum states to guide variable elimination.
Identify constraint classes closed under every elimination.
Efficiently construct feasible initial states and feasibility-preserving mixers for each reduced problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: Exact simulations on knapsack and vertex-weighted max-bisection instances show that the recursive scheme can outperform its non-recursive counterpart and penalty-based QAOA and RQAOA.
infographic.watch_item: Efficient constructions require restricted constraint structures; the abstract establishes simulation results, not practical quantum-hardware advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Recursive Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz

title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution
authors: Stefano Barison, Samuele Piccinelli, Alberto Baiardi, Francesco Tacchino, Ivano Tavernelli
abstract: Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under $\hat{S}^2$, and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. In classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and of an $[\text{Fe}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ model complex, and in experiments on an IBM quantum processor for the oxo-Mn(Salen) complex, this spin-adapted post-processing yields roots that are exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.

infographic.key_insight: Completing sampled electronic configurations restores spin symmetry in sample-based quantum diagonalization, yielding exact spin eigenfunctions even when spin-pure circuits alone cannot.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spin-adapted post-processing can reduce the classical diagonalization burden, with hardware results using subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than conventional constructions at the same circuit depth.
method: Use SqDRIFT with qDRIFT randomized time evolution to generate measurement samples.
Incorporate spin symmetry into initial-state preparation and time-evolution circuits.
Complete sampled configurations so the diagonalization subspace is closed under the total-spin operator S².
infographic.evidence_signal: Classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and an iron–ammine model complex, plus IBM hardware experiments on oxo-Mn(Salen), produced exact spin eigenfunctions at every evaluated subspace size.
infographic.watch_item: Exact spin symmetry does not guarantee energy accuracy; configuration-completion costs and sampling requirements still need assessment for larger systems.
infographic.paper_title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution

title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory
authors: Marie Kempkes, Jakob Spiegelberg, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum classifiers can represent predictive uncertainty by assigning belief weights to sets of labels, rather than only individual labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty-aware quantum predictions and offers a practical setting for evidence fusion with polynomial resource requirements.
method: Represent uncertainty using Dempster–Shafer mass assignments over label subsets.
Train parameterized quantum circuits to learn these assignments directly from data.
Prepare corresponding quantum states for post-processing, including quantum Dempster–Shafer fusion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a training framework and resource-efficiency claims but reports no datasets, numerical benchmarks, or uncertainty-quality metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Polynomial resource requirements for quantum fusion do not alone establish end-to-end practical advantage or reliable uncertainty estimates.
infographic.paper_title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory
